eyebrow: Quantum Error Correction & Fault Tolerance · Chapter 5
subtitle: Lesson 21 · Surface Code Fundamentals

eyebrow: The circuit: one ancilla, up to four CNOTs

steps.label: Each ancilla entangles to its up-to-4 neighboring data qubits
steps.sub: CNOT or CZ gates, structurally identical to Lesson 13's 2-CNOT circuit

steps.label: Then the ancilla is measured — 0 or 1
steps.sub: That bit is the stabilizer's syndrome for this round

steps.label: Every ancilla on the lattice runs in the same timestep
steps.sub: Not one stabilizer at a time — this is what makes it practical on real hardware

eyebrow: The new wrinkle: you can't trust one round

steps.label: A real data error flips a stabilizer and keeps it flipped
steps.sub: In every subsequent round, until corrected

steps.label: A faulty ancilla measurement flips it for just one round
steps.sub: The next round's measurement reverts to normal

steps.label: The pattern across time distinguishes the two cases
steps.sub: Not any single round in isolation

steps.label: This is why the surface code runs many rounds in a row
steps.sub: Protecting a logical qubit continuously, for as long as a computation runs

eyebrow: Defects in spacetime, not just in space

steps.label: A persistently triggered stabilizer outcome is a defect
steps.sub: 2D lattice position + round number = a 3D 'spacetime' picture

steps.label: Defects get paired up with another defect or the boundary
steps.sub: To identify the most likely underlying error chain

steps.label: That pairing problem is exactly what decoding solves
steps.sub: The subject of the next lesson

subtitle: Turning a lattice of flipped stabilizers into an actual correction, fast enough to matter.
